The proposed answer of 2/17 is correct, and the recursion and the closed form both check out.

**Recursion.** With n players left, the chance both Michael and James are chosen is C(n−2,2)/C(n,4) = 12/(n(n−1)), and they meet for certain. The chance exactly one is chosen is 2·C(n−2,3)/C(n,4) = 8(n−4)/(n(n−1)). That person must also win, with probability 1/4, so this case contributes 2(n−4)/(n(n−1)) · P(n−3). The chance neither is chosen is C(n−2,4)/C(n,4) = (n−4)(n−5)/(n(n−1)), and both then stay in the game. Adding the last two cases gives (n−4)(n−3)/(n(n−1)) · P(n−3), so P(n) = 12/(n(n−1)) + (n−4)(n−3)/(n(n−1)) · P(n−3).

**Closed form.** P(4) = 1 = 4/4. If P(n−3) = 4/(n−3), the recursion gives (12 + 4(n−4))/(n(n−1)) = 4(n−1)/(n(n−1)) = 4/n. By induction P(n) = 4/n for all n ≡ 1 mod 3, so P(34) = 4/34 = 2/17.

**Independent check.** The game has 11 rounds, and each round has C(4,2) = 6 pairs of players facing each other. That is 66 pairs meeting in total. By symmetry each of the C(34,2) = 561 pairs is equally likely to be one of them, so the probability is 66/561 = 2/17.

VERDICT: ACCEPT
